title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by international stories: a deadly factory fire in Indonesia, the collapse of the COP31 climate talks in Turkey without a main agreement, the capture of a cartel leader in Mexico, and the resignation of South Korea's education minister over AI-cheating measures. In the US, an ICE arrest at Seattle's airport set off a clash between state Democrats and federal officials, and a Delta system outage delayed flights at the start of Thanksgiving travel. Local Charlotte-area items and a North Korean marathon date change round out the brief.

stories.headline: Fire at Indonesian candy factory kills at least three; dozens missing
stories.summary: A fire broke out Saturday afternoon at the Fonusa Agung Mulia confectionery factory in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km west of Jakarta. At least three deaths are confirmed and dozens of workers remain unaccounted for. Police removed 24 body bags, which police said may contain remains of more than one person. Police say the victims cannot be identified visually and are collecting DNA from relatives, a process Fox News reported could take two to three weeks. The cause is under investigation, though survivors said the fire began in a cooling unit on the third floor, and the search was paused overnight and set to resume Monday.
key_facts: At least three people confirmed dead; 24 body bags recovered as of Sunday.
Four injured people were taken to a hospital and a clinic.
15 fire trucks were deployed, alongside police, military, Red Cross and volunteers.
The factory makes Milkita candies and is linked to Indonesian food company UNIFAM (United Family Food).
Firefighters said the building was already engulfed when they arrived, so they could not tell whether its fire protection system had worked.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian ran a straight wire-style account, emphasising the rescue effort, relatives waiting at the gate, the fire official's comment on the protection system, and Indonesia's record of deadly fires.

DW, CNA and the BBC focused on casualty counts, rescue operations and official quotes. DW and the BBC highlighted the 24 body bags and the expected rise in the death toll. DW explicitly raised questions about workplace safety standards.

Fox News gave the most detailed breakdown of worker numbers from the company, stressed the grim identification process and reignition risk, and also framed the fire as part of ongoing concern over workplace safety in Indonesia.

disputed: The number missing varies: 36 (CNA, Guardian, BBC), 37 (DW), 29 missing plus 8 unconfirmed (Fox, citing the factory), and about 50 unaccounted for (the factory owner, per Fox).
Estimates of how many were inside range from about 60 (the governor) to 65 in the affected area out of about 300 on site (the company).
Rescued survivors were given as 11 (DW) or 15 (BBC).
The cause is officially under investigation; the cooling-unit origin comes from survivors' accounts.
stories.why: The final death toll could be far higher than three, and the fire adds to scrutiny of industrial safety in Indonesia.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks end without main agreement after dispute over fossil fuel language
stories.summary: UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, ran nearly two days past their Friday deadline. They ended Sunday without the overarching 'cover decision' after the EU, UK, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Norway and others rejected a draft that did not mention fossil fuels. The draft, from the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, recalled the 2023 Dubai agreement to transition away from fossil fuels and set a goal of capturing and storing 1 billion metric tons of carbon. Russia and Saudi Arabia pushed to keep fossil fuels out of the text. Smaller decisions, including one on a 'just transition' for workers, were adopted, and UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was 'deeply disappointed.'
key_facts: The draft cover decision required near-unanimous consensus and was not adopted.
EU spokesman Darragh O'Brien, Ireland's minister: 'It's unconscionable that we would have a climate act that makes no reference to fossil fuels.'
The 10-page draft did not include the words fossil, oil, coal or phase out.
The talks ran roughly 44–48 hours overtime, which the AP describes as the longest ever.
Australia's Chris Bowen said the Dubai commitment remains in force and the energy transition is 'irreversible.'

perspectives.framing: The Guardian framed the result as a dramatic rejection, quoting O'Brien saying the EU would not accept a deal that 'greenwashes fossil fuels' and calling it a 'line in the sand'. It also quoted Power Shift Africa's Mohamed Adow accusing Europe of hypocrisy. PBS carried the AP account, adding context on accelerating warming, the Iran-war energy shock and El Niño.

The Korea Herald (AP) focused on procedural chaos: the three-hour objection window, the African Group's complaint and Kurum's hot-mic remark to Simon Stiell. DW highlighted developing-country campaigners blaming rich nations for blocking transition finance, and gave Russia's and Saudi Arabia's reasoning. The Hill led with Guterres's disappointment.

The Washington Examiner ran the same AP account as PBS, with nearly identical framing: the fossil fuel dispute, Russian and Saudi opposition, criticism of the presidencies, and Bowen's insistence the transition is happening.

disputed: Who bears blame is contested: some point to petrostates such as Russia and Saudi Arabia, while others, including campaigners quoted by DW and the Guardian, fault rich nations that expand fossil fuels and withhold transition finance.
The AP reported Kurum was absent when the failure was announced, while the Guardian quoted him acknowledging there was no consensus.
Carbon capture and storage remains disputed: Saudi Arabia says 'all solutions' are needed, while critics say it prolongs fossil fuel use.
stories.why: The breakdown leaves unclear whether the 2023 pledge to move away from fossil fuels will gain momentum as warming nears the Paris 1.5C threshold.

stories.headline: ICE arrests two on Seattle airport jet bridge, drawing governor's condemnation
stories.summary: On Saturday morning, masked ICE officers arrested Mexican national Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza on a jet bridge as passengers boarded Alaska Airlines flight 1306 to Los Angeles; ICE said he had overstayed a visa. ICE said a second woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, threw hot coffee at officers and would be charged with assaulting a federal officer; it said she had also overstayed a visa. Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called video of the arrests 'horrific' and 'chilling', said ICE is 'beyond reform', and urged airlines to ask ICE to leave state airports. DHS responded that 'this violence must end.' Alaska Airlines said it had no advance notice and is reviewing whether protocols were followed with the Port of Seattle.
key_facts: The arrests happened around 8 a.m. Saturday at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport during the busy pre-Thanksgiving travel period.
Flight 1306 was delayed about two hours and departed around 11 a.m.
Alaska Airlines: 'We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests.'
Ferguson said he believes the agents violated a state law he signed in March limiting face coverings for law enforcement.
ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, particularly of people who overstayed visas (PBS/AP).

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) emphasised the 'distressing' scene: video of a woman screaming that her daughter had a work permit, unmarked officers, Ferguson's call to abolish ICE, and the airline's and port's concerns. ICE's account of the coffee incident was included.
DW and The Hill led with Ferguson's criticism and the airline's concerns, and included ICE's account of the coffee-throwing and the assault charge.

Fox News framed the story as a clash between DHS and Democratic officials, foregrounding the alleged coffee assault and noting Ferguson did not mention it. It quoted DHS statistics on rising assaults on officers and Rep. Jayapal's 'fascist states' remark. The Washington Examiner used the term 'illegal immigrants' and gave both ICE's and Ferguson's statements.

disputed: The alleged coffee assault and claims that other passengers obstructed officers come from ICE/DHS and have not been independently verified.
DHS's figure for the increase in vehicular attacks appears as 300% in Fox News and 3,300% in the Washington Examiner.
Whether the agents broke Washington's face-covering law and how they reached the jet bridge are under review.
stories.why: The case sharpens the fight over immigration enforcement tactics at airports during peak travel and over state limits on federal agents.

stories.headline: Mexican forces capture alleged cartel leader 'El Chapo Isidro' in Sinaloa raid that left 11 dead
stories.summary: Mexican special forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader on the FBI's 10 most wanted list, in Guasave, Sinaloa, on Friday. The operation used US intelligence and was followed by heavy gunfire and vehicle fires across the region. Mexico's Defense Ministry said seven suspected gunmen and four soldiers were killed and eight people were detained, including his alleged second-in-command and his financial operator. Meza Flores was flown to Mexico City to face prosecution. The US, which had offered up to $5 million for information leading to his capture, is seeking his extradition.
key_facts: 11 dead: seven suspected gunmen and four soldiers.
Eight people were detained; weapons including a grenade launcher were seized, along with drugs and cash.
Meza Flores, 44, faces US drug trafficking charges filed in 2012 and 2019.
He was formerly part of the Beltrán Leyva organisation and set up his own group by 2013.
The US consulate in Hermosillo warned of clashes, road blockades and vehicle fires across several Sinaloa towns.

perspectives.framing: Al Jazeera gave a detailed explainer on how the raid was planned, citing The New York Times on US drone surveillance, intercepted communications and diversionary raids. The Guardian US ran video of burning vehicles on highways.

The Korea Herald (AP) stressed the terror felt by Guasave residents and experts' warnings that removing leaders can trigger more violence, noting Trump's pressure on Mexico. The BBC focused on official details of the arrests and US charges, and on the consulate warning.

disputed: The group's name differs across reports: Los Mazatlecos, the Meza Flores Organisation/Guasave Cartel, or the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization.
Details of US involvement, such as drone surveillance, come largely from The New York Times as cited by Al Jazeera; Mexico gave few specifics.
Whether the capture will lead to more violence among warring Sinaloa factions is uncertain.
stories.why: The arrest is a high-profile result of US-Mexico security cooperation but could fuel further violence in an already contested region.

stories.headline: South Korea's education minister resigns over last-minute anti-AI cheating measures for college exam
stories.summary: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned Sunday, and President Lee Jae Myung accepted. The resignation followed criticism of hastily imposed rules meant to stop AI-assisted cheating on the Suneung college entrance exam held Thursday. The measures followed a confession by the top scorer in a national tax accountancy exam that he had used a hidden camera, a smartphone and AI. They included pencil-only rules, stickers over clothing buttons, blocked public Wi-Fi, and three nationwide emergency phone alerts during the exam. Choi said he could not escape criticism that the ministry had failed to prepare. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook was told to handle follow-up measures, and a successor will be nominated.
key_facts: 111 suspected cases of cheating involving electronic devices were detected; nearly half were found through the emergency alerts (CNA).
About 500,000 students took the Suneung (BBC).
Asked in parliament whether he was confident cheaters could be caught, Choi, 72, said he was not, citing his age.
It was the first time South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters (BBC).

perspectives.framing: The Guardian detailed the crackdown, including a reward of at least $75,000 for reporting cheating, and noted that teachers' unions called the response belated. It set the story in the context of how central the exam is to Korean life.

Yonhap, the BBC and CNA reported the resignation and the measures in similar terms. Yonhap also noted that a perfect scorer on the law school entrance test was found dead after cheating allegations. The BBC highlighted the anxiety honest test takers felt, for example about their glasses.

disputed: Police are still investigating cheating allegations tied to the law school entrance exam case.
stories.why: The episode shows how AI tools are straining high-stakes testing and how governments may struggle to respond.

stories.headline: Opinion: Fox News piece criticises Justice Department's stance on AI training and copyright
stories.summary: A Fox News opinion article criticises a Justice Department statement of interest in the copyright lawsuit brought by The New York Times and other news organizations against OpenAI and Microsoft. According to the piece, the DOJ backed OpenAI's argument that training AI on copyrighted articles is 'fair use', citing costs to developers and US AI leadership. The author argues this departs from more balanced White House and G20 guidance, could favour large AI firms over startups, and conflicts with property rights.
key_facts: News organizations including The New York Times are suing OpenAI and Microsoft over the use of their articles in AI training.
The DOJ filed a statement of interest supporting the fair use argument, according to the piece.
The article cites the White House AI framework and the G20 'Carolina Principles', which call copyright an 'essential' protection.

perspectives.framing: This is an opinion piece arguing from a property-rights view against the DOJ's position. It frames the dispute as a split within the Trump administration and argues that licensing helps startups.

disputed: This is a single opinion piece; the DOJ's reasoning is presented only through the author's characterisation.
The fair use question is unresolved in court.
stories.why: How courts and the government treat AI training on copyrighted work will shape both the AI industry and publishers.

links.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners

stories.headline: Delta system outage delays flights in Atlanta and nationwide as Thanksgiving travel begins
stories.summary: A failure in Delta Air Lines' automated weight-and-balance system on Sunday morning led to a brief ground stop for Atlanta-bound Delta flights. The FAA then replaced it with a ground delay running until about 1 p.m. Delta said staff were using manual workarounds while it restored automation, and the FAA said the problem was not related to its air traffic systems. Delays spread to other airports, including Los Angeles, San Francisco and several East Coast hubs. The outage came about a week after a separate FAA failure caused a nationwide ground stop.
key_facts: The ground stop began at 7:46 a.m. ET and was replaced with a ground delay around 8:30–8:40 a.m.
The ground delay averaged about 57 minutes, with a maximum of 111 minutes (Newsweek).
By midday, FlightAware showed 835 delays at Atlanta and 725 Delta flights delayed nationwide (New York Post).
Hartsfield-Jackson expects more than 4 million passengers between Nov. 19 and Dec. 1.

perspectives.framing: The Verge gave a short report, linking the outage to the previous week's nationwide ground stop and explaining the weight-and-balance system.
Newsweek and WBTV took a service-oriented approach, giving the timeline, the cause and passenger rebooking and refund guidance, and noting the holiday travel volume.

The New York Post used 'chaos' framing focused on California airports and linked the outage to recent Delta safety incidents. Fox News stressed the FAA's statement that its systems were not at fault and mentioned recent cybersecurity concerns. The Washington Examiner carried a brief AP item.

disputed: Fox News reported at least 3,500 Delta flights 'reportedly' delayed, while the New York Post said the FAA warned 3,500 flights 'could be affected'. Other delay counts are much lower.
When the automated system was fully restored was not reported.
stories.why: Holiday travellers face disruption, and the outage adds to concerns about the reliability of aviation technology.

stories.headline: Man charged after shooting during argument in Huntersville
stories.summary: Huntersville police responded to the 9200 block of Toledo Road around 9:21 p.m. Saturday and found a man with a gunshot wound to the leg. Police say Sergio Vanegas fired several rounds during an argument involving a large group, and one round hit the victim. Vanegas was arrested without incident and charged with assault with a deadly weapon inflicting serious injury. The victim is in stable condition.
key_facts: The victim is in stable condition at a local hospital.
The charge is assault with a deadly weapon inflicting serious injury.
Vanegas was taken to Mecklenburg County Jail.

perspectives.framing: Local TV outlets reported the police account directly, along with tip-line information.

disputed: WCNC's timing of the arrest ('shortly after 9 p.m.') does not match the 9:21 p.m. police response time reported elsewhere.
stories.why: It is a local public safety incident in the Charlotte area, and police are seeking information.

stories.headline: North Korea moves Pyongyang marathon from April to October 2027, tour agency says
stories.summary: Beijing-based Koryo Tours, the event's exclusive travel partner, said the 2027 Pyongyang International Marathon will not be held in April and will 'almost certainly' take place in October, likely Oct. 3. The race has been held since 1981 to mark Kim Il-sung's April 15 birthday. No reason was given. This year's April race was cancelled about a month beforehand.
key_facts: First held in 1981; opened to foreign amateur runners in 2014.
The race was suspended 2020–2024 due to COVID and returned in 2025 with about 200 foreign runners.
The exact date has not yet been confirmed.

perspectives.framing: All outlets relied on the Koryo Tours announcement. The Korea Herald added context on major April 2027 anniversaries but noted it is unclear whether they played a role.

disputed: The reason for the change is unknown, and the October date is not final.
stories.why: It is a small but notable break from a political tradition at one of North Korea's few events open to foreigners.

stories.headline: Pedestrian killed in hit-and-run on South Tryon Street in Charlotte
stories.summary: Police say 59-year-old Ada Dennis was struck and killed Friday evening while crossing South Tryon Street in a marked crosswalk near Shops at Whitehall Commons. Witnesses said a large black pickup truck hit her and drove off, and the driver has not been identified. Police do not believe speed was a factor. The investigation is active, and police are asking for tips through Crime Stoppers.
key_facts: The crash happened around 6:34 p.m. on Nov. 20.
The victim was crossing in a marked crosswalk, according to police.
It is one of several recent pedestrian crashes in the region, including another deadly one near Arrowood Road on Nov. 11.

perspectives.framing: WBTV set the crash in the context of a string of recent pedestrian deaths and city council proposals on street safety; WCNC gave a brief report.

disputed: The driver has not been identified, and it is unclear whether impairment was involved.
stories.why: It adds to growing concern about pedestrian safety in south Charlotte.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: No articles in this edition directly address US or EU AI regulation. A related item is a Fox News opinion piece (story s6) criticising the Justice Department's support for treating AI training on copyrighted material as fair use.
